title: E2B Pricing: Plans, Rates and Limits (2026 Guide)
summary: E2B pricing has multiple tiers with per-unit execution costs and resource limits. Review rates and plan features to select an appropriate plan.
body_markdown:
## Hidden costs and limits E2B users hit first


Four limits bite first: the session cap, the concurrency ceiling, billing that runs for as long as a sandbox is running, and sandbox size. Add to those the cleanup code you end up writing yourself.


Before you design around any of them, read the exact values on E2B's pricing and docs pages for your plan. Each limit moves either your bill or your architecture.


### E2B session length and concurrency limits


When a job outlasts the session cap, which is far shorter on Hobby than on Pro, it can't be one sandbox on Hobby. You have to checkpoint state and start a fresh sandbox, which is extra code and extra startup time per job.


Hobby also limits how many sandboxes can run at once. Past that ceiling, new requests are refused, so a traffic spike becomes failed user requests unless you add a queue. Moving to Pro raises both limits, and that raises your floor cost too.


### E2B charges for idle sandboxes


You pay for the time a sandbox is running, not the time it's doing work. An agent waiting on a user's reply, a slow model call or a human approval step is still on the meter if the sandbox is up.


> You pay for the time a sandbox is running, not the time it's doing work.


So a long wait inside a session costs the same as a long computation.


If your workflow pauses often, shut the sandbox down between steps and rebuild state when work resumes, rather than assuming quiet time is free.


### Larger sandboxes multiplying the rate


You can match the machine to the job with custom CPU and RAM sizing, but the per-second rate rises with the size you choose.


Setting every sandbox to the largest size to be safe multiplies your whole bill by the same factor. Size to the heaviest realistic task, then test whether lighter jobs can run smaller.


Because the signup credit is one-time, it won't cover that experimenting for long. Treat it as a trial budget and not a recurring allowance.


### Orphaned E2B sandboxes and cleanup


Lose track of a sandbox and it keeps running and keeps billing. Retries cause most orphans. If a request times out and your code retries, the first sandbox may still be alive while the second starts.


Give every sandbox a tag tied to the job that created it, and set a timeout so it ends itself. Run a periodic sweep that lists live sandboxes and kills any with no matching job.


Activepieces can run that sweep on a timer, and if the E2B call you need isn't in its catalogue, you can build the missing integration yourself and keep it in your own instance instead of waiting on a vendor release.


About 60% of its 746 integrations are community-contributed, counted straight from the open-source monorepo on GitHub, and the core is MIT-licensed.


Log creation and teardown for each one, because without those records you can't tell a leak from legitimate load when the invoice arrives.
